reference_text:
Welcome to the course. We will work through each concept carefully, connect the
ideas step by step, and use practical examples to make technical topics easier
to understand. When we introduce a new method, focus first on the problem it
solves and why it is useful. For example, in machine learning, features are the
information we give the model, while the target is what we want it to predict.
Now consider a simple question: what changes when the data contains missing
values? We will think through the reason and then look at the code. In Python,
we can inspect the data, run one small step at a time, and explain what the
result means. The goal is to understand the logic, not simply memorize syntax.

slides.title: Start
slides.transcript: Welcome to Module 12, Views and Modular Queries. This module is about turning useful SQL logic into reusable database interfaces. We will learn standard views, materialized views, updatable views, check options, dependency inspection, freshness policies, and modular query design. The central idea is that a view is not just saved text. It is an interface with a row grain, a set of columns, and a meaning that downstream users may depend on. Keep a real project in mind as we work through this section—for example, an analytics team exposing a stable reporting view to dashboard users. The technical feature matters because it changes what questions we can answer reliably and how easily another analyst can understand our work. As you listen, try to connect each SQL or data concept to a decision you might need to defend later: what the data means, what one row represents, what can be missing, and what assumptions the transformation introduces.

slides.title: Why views matter
slides.transcript: Views solve several problems at once. They let us centralize shared SQL logic. They create a stable interface with deliberate columns and row meaning. They can reduce accidental exposure by omitting unnecessary fields, although actual authorization still depends on database security controls. And materialized views can store reusable results when freshness does not need to be immediate. A standard view stores a query definition, not a separate copy of the rows. Treat the selected columns, names, types, and grain as a contract with downstream users. Changing that contract can break dashboards or applications even if the underlying query still runs.

slides.title: Learning goals
slides.transcript: By the end of this module, you should be able to create standard views, inspect their definitions and dependencies, explain when a view is updatable, and use a check option to control writes through a filtered view. You should also understand materialized-view freshness and be able to decide whether logic belongs in a statement-level CTE, a reusable standard view, or a stored materialized result. Keep a real project in mind as we work through this section—for example, a governance project limiting which columns different users can access. The technical feature matters because it changes what questions we can answer reliably and how easily another analyst can understand our work. As you listen, try to connect each SQL or data concept to a decision you might need to defend later: what the data means, what one row represents, what can be missing, and what assumptions the transformation introduces.

slides.title: Module roadmap
slides.transcript: We will start with modularity and standard views. Then we will inspect reusable objects and their dependencies. After that, we will explore controlled writes and access boundaries. Materialized views come next, with a focus on freshness and refresh policy. Finally, we will combine views and CTEs into a small reusable analytics layer. Keep a real project in mind as we work through this section—for example, an analytics team exposing a stable reporting view to dashboard users. The technical feature matters because it changes what questions we can answer reliably and how easily another analyst can understand our work. As you listen, try to connect each SQL or data concept to a decision you might need to defend later: what the data means, what one row represents, what can be missing, and what assumptions the transformation introduces.

slides.title: Teaching database
slides.transcript: The database contains a few small source areas. Patient and admission tables support healthcare-style views. Employee, department, and sales-order tables support a performance interface. Customer transactions support recent-activity and retention examples. Reusable objects are placed in an analytics schema so the source tables and analytical interfaces are clearly separated. Connect this idea to a data platform materializing expensive summaries for faster consumption. Ask what could go wrong if the concept were misunderstood: could rows be duplicated, important records disappear, categories be interpreted incorrectly, or a report become difficult to reproduce? A strong analyst can explain both the SQL operation and the assumption behind it. After the example, summarize the idea in one plain-language sentence before moving on.

slides.title: Modular architecture
slides.transcript: Modularity works best when each layer has one responsibility. Base tables store source facts. A shared view can own stable relational logic. A report-level CTE can own a temporary threshold, ranking rule, or sequence calculation. The final query produces the consumer-specific result. This separation makes each layer easier to test and change. Choose the smallest reusable object that matches the need. A CTE is local to one query, a view centralizes live logic, and a materialized view persists a snapshot. Promote logic into shared objects when it is stable, reused, and worth governing as part of the analytical architecture.

slides.title: Three reusable choices
slides.transcript: The three main choices in this module differ in lifetime and storage. A CTE exists for one statement. A standard view is a persistent database object, but it stores the query definition rather than a result snapshot. A materialized view is persistent and stores the query result. Choose among them based on reuse, freshness, and computational cost. Connect this idea to an analytics team exposing a stable reporting view to dashboard users. Ask what could go wrong if the concept were misunderstood: could rows be duplicated, important records disappear, categories be interpreted incorrectly, or a report become difficult to reproduce? A strong analyst can explain both the SQL operation and the assumption behind it. After the example, summarize the idea in one plain-language sentence before moving on.

slides.title: What a standard view stores
slides.transcript: A standard view stores a query definition. It does not normally store a separate snapshot of the result. When the view is queried, PostgreSQL uses the view definition to access current underlying data. For consumers, the view behaves like a named relation with columns and rows. A standard view stores a query definition, not a separate copy of the rows. Treat the selected columns, names, types, and grain as a contract with downstream users. Changing that contract can break dashboards or applications even if the underlying query still runs.

slides.title: View contract
slides.transcript: Think of a view as a contract. The object name matters. The exposed columns and types matter. The row grain matters. And consumers should understand how fresh the data is. If you change a shared view in a way that breaks one of these expectations, downstream queries can fail or change meaning. A standard view stores a query definition, not a separate copy of the rows. Treat the selected columns, names, types, and grain as a contract with downstream users. Changing that contract can break dashboards or applications even if the underlying query still runs.

slides.title: Explore database objects
slides.transcript: Run the schema exploration query first. Look at objects in the public and analytics schemas. The public schema contains source tables. The analytics schema contains reusable interfaces. This separation is helpful because object location can communicate purpose. Choose the smallest reusable object that matches the need. A CTE is local to one query, a view centralizes live logic, and a materialized view persists a snapshot. Promote logic into shared objects when it is stable, reused, and worth governing as part of the analytical architecture.

slides.title: Query a view
slides.transcript: This query reads the patient-admission summary view. Consumers do not need to repeat the join or stay-duration expression. The view already defines that interface. Run it and identify the grain. One row represents one admission with selected patient attributes and a derived stay duration. When reading the example, do not read punctuation one character at a time. Start with the purpose of the query, then identify the input rows, the operation being applied, and the shape of the expected output. In a real setting such as a data platform materializing expensive summaries for faster consumption, this habit makes code reviews much easier because you can explain what the query is supposed to guarantee before discussing syntax. After running it, inspect a few records manually and check that the result matches that explanation.

slides.title: Create a view
slides.transcript: Before creating a view, make four decisions. Choose a meaningful name. Define the row grain. Choose the columns intentionally. Then write the SELECT that implements that interface. Starting with the contract makes the SQL easier to evaluate. When reading the example, do not read punctuation one character at a time. Start with the purpose of the query, then identify the input rows, the operation being applied, and the shape of the expected output. In a real setting such as a governance project limiting which columns different users can access, this habit makes code reviews much easier because you can explain what the query is supposed to guarantee before discussing syntax. After running it, inspect a few records manually and check that the result matches that explanation.

slides.title: CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW
slides.transcript: CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW lets you update a compatible view definition without first dropping the object. This is useful when the interface should remain available under the same name. But compatibility matters. Changing column names, meanings, types, or grain can still affect downstream users, even if the SQL command succeeds. When reading the example, do not read punctuation one character at a time. Start with the purpose of the query, then identify the input rows, the operation being applied, and the shape of the expected output. In a real setting such as an analytics team exposing a stable reporting view to dashboard users, this habit makes code reviews much easier because you can explain what the query is supposed to guarantee before discussing syntax. After running it, inspect a few records manually and check that the result matches that explanation.

slides.title: Use the view for aggregation
slides.transcript: Once the patient-admission interface exists, later reports can start from it. This query groups the reusable admission rows by department. The report author does not need to repeat patient joins or stay-duration calculations. That is the value of modular SQL: stable logic is centralized, and consumer queries become smaller. A standard view stores a query definition, not a separate copy of the rows. Treat the selected columns, names, types, and grain as a contract with downstream users. Changing that contract can break dashboards or applications even if the underlying query still runs.

slides.title: Naming conventions
slides.transcript: This course uses vw as a prefix for standard views and mv for materialized views. PostgreSQL does not require that naming convention. The goal is readability and discoverability. Whatever convention a team chooses, use it consistently and document the intended grain and meaning of important shared objects. Connect this idea to a governance project limiting which columns different users can access. Ask what could go wrong if the concept were misunderstood: could rows be duplicated, important records disappear, categories be interpreted incorrectly, or a report become difficult to reproduce? A strong analyst can explain both the SQL operation and the assumption behind it. After the example, summarize the idea in one plain-language sentence before moving on.

slides.title: Inspect view definitions
slides.transcript: Shared database objects should not be mysterious. PostgreSQL's information schema can show view names and definitions. Run this query and inspect the SQL behind the analytics views. Being able to inspect a view helps with debugging, documentation, and change review. A standard view stores a query definition, not a separate copy of the rows. Treat the selected columns, names, types, and grain as a contract with downstream users. Changing that contract can break dashboards or applications even if the underlying query still runs.

slides.title: Inspect dependencies
slides.transcript: A shared view depends on other database objects. This query uses information schema metadata to show which tables feed each view. Dependency awareness matters because changing a base object or shared view can affect several downstream consumers. Before making a breaking change, understand the dependency chain. Reusable SQL objects create dependencies. Before changing a base view, identify which other views, reports, or applications depend on it. Good change management includes version awareness, tests, and communication—not just editing CREATE VIEW until it succeeds.

slides.title: Dependency chain
slides.transcript: A view can sit in the middle of a dependency chain. Base tables feed the shared interface. A report-specific CTE reads the view. A report consumes the final result. If the view grain or column meaning changes, every downstream layer may be affected. Treat important shared views as versioned contracts, not disposable snippets. Reusable SQL objects create dependencies. Before changing a base view, identify which other views, reports, or applications depend on it. Good change management includes version awareness, tests, and communication—not just editing CREATE VIEW until it succeeds.

slides.title: Change management
slides.transcript: Change management goes beyond syntax. A CREATE OR REPLACE command may succeed, but a semantic change can still break analytics. Consumers may depend on a column name, data type, business definition, or row grain. Review those contract elements before changing a shared object. Reusable SQL objects create dependencies. Before changing a base view, identify which other views, reports, or applications depend on it. Good change management includes version awareness, tests, and communication—not just editing CREATE VIEW until it succeeds.

slides.title: Simple views can be updatable
slides.transcript: Some simple PostgreSQL views are automatically updatable. A write through the view can flow to the underlying table. But this is not true for every view. Joins, aggregates, grouping, and other features can make a view non-updatable. Treat writable views as a deliberate interface and test their behavior. A standard view stores a query definition, not a separate copy of the rows. Treat the selected columns, names, types, and grain as a contract with downstream users. Changing that contract can break dashboards or applications even if the underlying query still runs.

slides.title: Update through a view
slides.transcript: This example updates city through a simple active-patient view. RETURNING shows the changed row. The transaction then rolls back, so the demonstration does not permanently modify the teaching database. This is a good pattern when learning or testing write behavior. A standard view stores a query definition, not a separate copy of the rows. Treat the selected columns, names, types, and grain as a contract with downstream users. Changing that contract can break dashboards or applications even if the underlying query still runs.

slides.title: Filtered updatable view
slides.transcript: A filtered view introduces an important write question. If the view only shows active patients, what should happen when an update through the view sets active to false? Without a check option, the row may simply disappear from the view after the update. WITH CHECK OPTION can enforce the view condition for writes performed through the view. A standard view stores a query definition, not a separate copy of the rows. Treat the selected columns, names, types, and grain as a contract with downstream users. Changing that contract can break dashboards or applications even if the underlying query still runs.

slides.title: WITH CHECK OPTION
slides.transcript: WITH CHECK OPTION enforces the view's filter for writes through the view. If an update would make a row no longer satisfy the active equals true condition, PostgreSQL rejects the write. This turns the filtered view into a more controlled write interface. It does not replace general database constraints or permissions. Some simple views can be updated because PostgreSQL can map each view row back to one base-table row. Filtered views introduce a policy question: should an update be allowed to move a row outside the view? WITH CHECK OPTION prevents writes that violate the view's own filter.

slides.title: CHECK OPTION failure
slides.transcript: This example intentionally fails. The active-patient view shows only active rows and includes a check option. The update tries to set an active patient to inactive through that view. Because the resulting row would no longer satisfy the view condition, PostgreSQL rejects the update. This is expected behavior. Some simple views can be updated because PostgreSQL can map each view row back to one base-table row. Filtered views introduce a policy question: should an update be allowed to move a row outside the view? WITH CHECK OPTION prevents writes that violate the view's own filter.

slides.title: Do not infer writability
slides.transcript: Do not assume every view is writable. A simple one-table view may support automatic updates. A join or aggregate view does not have the same direct row mapping. Materialized views are stored query results, not ordinary write-through interfaces. Always check the actual PostgreSQL behavior for the view definition you are designing. Ask what could go wrong if the concept were misunderstood: could rows be duplicated, important records disappear, categories be interpreted incorrectly, or a report become difficult to reproduce? A strong analyst can explain both the SQL operation and the assumption behind it. After the example, summarize the idea in one plain-language sentence before moving on.

slides.title: Views as access boundaries
slides.transcript: A view can reduce accidental exposure by publishing only the columns required for an analytical task. For example, an analytics interface may expose an age band and city instead of direct contact fields. But hiding columns in a view definition is not the same as granting or denying access. Actual authorization depends on PostgreSQL privileges and, where appropriate, row-level security or other controls. A standard view stores a query definition, not a separate copy of the rows. Treat the selected columns, names, types, and grain as a contract with downstream users. Changing that contract can break dashboards or applications even if the underlying query still runs.

slides.title: Limited analytics view
slides.transcript: This analytics view exposes subject ID, age band, city, and active status. It omits name, email, and date of birth. That creates a narrower analytical interface. Run it and compare the result with the source patient table. The design reduces unnecessary fields, but access to objects must still be configured separately. A standard view stores a query definition, not a separate copy of the rows. Treat the selected columns, names, types, and grain as a contract with downstream users. Changing that contract can break dashboards or applications even if the underlying query still runs.

slides.title: security_invoker
slides.transcript: PostgreSQL supports a security invoker option for views. With security invoker, permissions on underlying relations are checked using the invoking user's rights. This can matter in a real multi-role security design. Our browser lab is useful for syntax and object behavior, but it does not reproduce a full production authorization environment. Views can reduce exposure by presenting only approved columns or rows, but they are not a complete security strategy by themselves. Understand ownership, privileges, and whether the view executes with invoker or definer-like behavior. Sensitive data controls should be explicit and tested.

slides.title: security_invoker SQL
slides.transcript: This query recreates the patient analytics view with security invoker enabled. It still exposes the same selected analytical columns. The key difference is how PostgreSQL evaluates underlying access permissions. In a production environment, you would test this with real roles and grants. When reading the example, do not read punctuation one character at a time. Start with the purpose of the query, then identify the input rows, the operation being applied, and the shape of the expected output. In a real setting such as a data platform materializing expensive summaries for faster consumption, this habit makes code reviews much easier because you can explain what the query is supposed to guarantee before discussing syntax. After running it, inspect a few records manually and check that the result matches that explanation.

slides.title: Security boundaries
slides.transcript: Views are useful security-adjacent interfaces, but they should not be described as secure or compliant simply because they hide columns. Permissions still matter. Row-level security may matter. Application access paths matter. Compliance depends on a broader system of controls. Keep the claim proportional to what the view actually does. Views can reduce exposure by presenting only approved columns or rows, but they are not a complete security strategy by themselves. Understand ownership, privileges, and whether the view executes with invoker or definer-like behavior. Sensitive data controls should be explicit and tested.

slides.title: Materialized views
slides.transcript: A materialized view is fundamentally different from a standard view. The materialized view stores query results. That can make repeated reads of an expensive summary convenient. But the stored result can become stale as base tables change. Freshness therefore becomes part of the object's contract. A standard view stores a query definition, not a separate copy of the rows. Treat the selected columns, names, types, and grain as a contract with downstream users. Changing that contract can break dashboards or applications even if the underlying query still runs.

slides.title: When materialization helps
slides.transcript: Materialization is useful when an expensive result is read repeatedly and consumers can tolerate a known refresh lag. The database object alone is not the whole design. You also need a refresh schedule, freshness metadata, and a plan for refresh failures. Without those, consumers may not know how current the snapshot is. Connect this idea to a data platform materializing expensive summaries for faster consumption. Ask what could go wrong if the concept were misunderstood: could rows be duplicated, important records disappear, categories be interpreted incorrectly, or a report become difficult to reproduce? A strong analyst can explain both the SQL operation and the assumption behind it. After the example, summarize the idea in one plain-language sentence before moving on.

slides.title: Create materialized view
slides.transcript: This query creates a diagnosis summary materialized view. The result has one row per diagnosis. It stores admission count, distinct patient count, average stay, and a refresh timestamp. The refresh timestamp documents when the snapshot was generated. It does not update every time someone reads the materialized view. When reading the example, do not read punctuation one character at a time. Start with the purpose of the query, then identify the input rows, the operation being applied, and the shape of the expected output. In a real setting such as a governance project limiting which columns different users can access, this habit makes code reviews much easier because you can explain what the query is supposed to guarantee before discussing syntax. After running it, inspect a few records manually and check that the result matches that explanation.

slides.title: Materialized view grain
slides.transcript: Materialized views still need a clear grain. In this example, one row represents one diagnosis. The measures summarize admissions for that diagnosis. The refreshed-at value records when the stored result was produced. Consumers need both the grain and freshness information to interpret the data correctly. A standard view stores a query definition, not a separate copy of the rows. Treat the selected columns, names, types, and grain as a contract with downstream users. Changing that contract can break dashboards or applications even if the underlying query still runs.

slides.title: Query the snapshot
slides.transcript: Once the materialized view exists, consumers can query the stored summary directly. The consuming query is simple because the aggregation has already been computed. But remember that the result is only as fresh as the last successful refresh. When reading the example, do not read punctuation one character at a time. Start with the purpose of the query, then identify the input rows, the operation being applied, and the shape of the expected output. In a real setting such as a data platform materializing expensive summaries for faster consumption, this habit makes code reviews much easier because you can explain what the query is supposed to guarantee before discussing syntax. After running it, inspect a few records manually and check that the result matches that explanation.

slides.title: Freshness timeline
slides.transcript: Materialized-view freshness is easiest to understand as a timeline. The snapshot is built. Later, a new base-table row arrives. The standard base query can see it immediately, but the materialized view does not. After a refresh, the stored snapshot catches up. That delay must be documented for users. A materialized view stores the query result physically, trading freshness for faster reads. That makes refresh policy part of the data contract. A dashboard should know whether the snapshot is five minutes old or one day old. Indexes can improve access, and concurrent refresh has additional requirements.

slides.title: Create stale snapshot demo
slides.transcript: This example inserts another Influenza admission into the base table. Then it compares the live base-table count with the stored materialized-view count. The base table changes immediately. The snapshot remains unchanged because it has not been refreshed. This demonstrates staleness directly. When reading the example, do not read punctuation one character at a time. Start with the purpose of the query, then identify the input rows, the operation being applied, and the shape of the expected output. In a real setting such as an analytics team exposing a stable reporting view to dashboard users, this habit makes code reviews much easier because you can explain what the query is supposed to guarantee before discussing syntax. After running it, inspect a few records manually and check that the result matches that explanation.

slides.title: Refresh materialized view
slides.transcript: REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW recomputes the stored result from the underlying query. Run this after creating the stale condition. The Influenza count should now match the current base data. The refreshed-at value should also be recomputed, documenting the new snapshot time. A standard view stores a query definition, not a separate copy of the rows. Treat the selected columns, names, types, and grain as a contract with downstream users. Changing that contract can break dashboards or applications even if the underlying query still runs.

slides.title: Freshness is a contract
slides.transcript: Freshness policy is part of the data product. Consumers need to know how often the materialized view refreshes. They need a way to see the last successful refresh. The team should know what happens when refresh fails. And the expected maximum latency should be documented rather than assumed. A standard view stores a query definition, not a separate copy of the rows. Treat the selected columns, names, types, and grain as a contract with downstream users. Changing that contract can break dashboards or applications even if the underlying query still runs.

slides.title: Index a materialized view
slides.transcript: Because a materialized view stores rows, PostgreSQL can index those rows. This example creates a unique index on diagnosis. Indexes may support faster reads and are also relevant to certain PostgreSQL concurrent refresh requirements. Choose indexes based on real query patterns and constraints, not simply because the object is materialized. A standard view stores a query definition, not a separate copy of the rows. Treat the selected columns, names, types, and grain as a contract with downstream users. Changing that contract can break dashboards or applications even if the underlying query still runs.

slides.title: Concurrent refresh note
slides.transcript: Production PostgreSQL supports REFRESH MATERIALIZED VIEW CONCURRENTLY under specific conditions. An appropriate unique index is required. Concurrent refresh is an availability technique. It does not remove the need for a refresh policy, freshness metadata, or monitoring. A materialized view stores the query result physically, trading freshness for faster reads. That makes refresh policy part of the data contract. A dashboard should know whether the snapshot is five minutes old or one day old. Indexes can improve access, and concurrent refresh has additional requirements.

slides.title: Compare live and snapshot
slides.transcript: A useful monitoring pattern is to compare the live result with the stored snapshot. This query shows diagnosis counts from both sources. After a successful refresh, the values should agree for the same logic. If they differ unexpectedly, investigate whether the snapshot is stale or the definitions are inconsistent. A materialized view stores the query result physically, trading freshness for faster reads. That makes refresh policy part of the data contract. A dashboard should know whether the snapshot is five minutes old or one day old. Indexes can improve access, and concurrent refresh has additional requirements.

slides.title: CTE vs view vs materialized view
slides.transcript: This comparison helps choose the right object. A CTE is local to one statement. A standard view is shared and live. A materialized view is shared and stored. Temporary business thresholds usually belong close to the report. Stable shared relational meaning often belongs in a standard view. Expensive reused summaries may justify materialization if the freshness tradeoff is acceptable. A standard view stores a query definition, not a separate copy of the rows. Treat the selected columns, names, types, and grain as a contract with downstream users. Changing that contract can break dashboards or applications even if the underlying query still runs.

slides.title: Promote only stable logic
slides.transcript: A useful architecture rule is to promote stable meaning into persistent objects. If many consumers agree on what a patient-admission row means, that can become a view. If one report uses a temporary thirty-day threshold, keep that logic in the report. If a summary is expensive and reused frequently, materialization may be appropriate. Do not turn every query into a database object. Choose the smallest reusable object that matches the need. A CTE is local to one query, a view centralizes live logic, and a materialized view persists a snapshot. Promote logic into shared objects when it is stable, reused, and worth governing as part of the analytical architecture.

slides.title: View + CTE
slides.transcript: This query combines Modules 11 and 12. The view owns the stable patient-admission interface. The CTEs own report-specific sequence and readmission logic. LAG calculates the previous discharge. The final threshold checks whether the gap is within thirty days. This separation keeps the stable data interface reusable while allowing reports to define their own analytical rules. A standard view stores a query definition, not a separate copy of the rows. Treat the selected columns, names, types, and grain as a contract with downstream users. Changing that contract can break dashboards or applications even if the underlying query still runs.

slides.title: Project architecture
slides.transcript: The project asks you to design a small analytics layer for three needs. Employee performance is stable shared logic and fits a standard view. Recent customer activity can be a shared view, while the at-risk threshold remains in a CTE because it may vary by report. The diagnosis dashboard uses a repeated summary and can use a materialized view when a refresh delay is acceptable. Choose the smallest reusable object that matches the need. A CTE is local to one query, a view centralizes live logic, and a materialized view persists a snapshot. Promote logic into shared objects when it is stable, reused, and worth governing as part of the analytical architecture.

slides.title: Employee performance view
slides.transcript: This view joins employees to departments and sales orders. It aggregates orders and sales amount. One output row represents one employee. Because this definition can support several operations reports, publishing it as a reusable view is reasonable. A standard view stores a query definition, not a separate copy of the rows. Treat the selected columns, names, types, and grain as a contract with downstream users. Changing that contract can break dashboards or applications even if the underlying query still runs.

slides.title: Consume employee view
slides.transcript: This query consumes the employee performance interface. The total-sales threshold remains outside the view. That is useful because different reports may choose different thresholds. The stable performance definition stays shared, while temporary business rules remain report-specific. A standard view stores a query definition, not a separate copy of the rows. Treat the selected columns, names, types, and grain as a contract with downstream users. Changing that contract can break dashboards or applications even if the underlying query still runs.

slides.title: Recent activity view
slides.transcript: The recent-activity view publishes completed transactions from a defined six-month window. That shared definition can support multiple retention analyses. It creates a smaller, clearer interface than asking every report author to repeat the transaction-status logic. A standard view stores a query definition, not a separate copy of the rows. Treat the selected columns, names, types, and grain as a contract with downstream users. Changing that contract can break dashboards or applications even if the underlying query still runs.

slides.title: Retention CTE
slides.transcript: This retention query starts from the recent-activity view. A CTE finds the last transaction per customer. Another CTE applies a sixty-day inactivity threshold. That threshold is intentionally report-specific. If another report wants ninety days, the shared activity view does not need to change. Ask what could go wrong if the concept were misunderstood: could rows be duplicated, important records disappear, categories be interpreted incorrectly, or a report become difficult to reproduce? A strong analyst can explain both the SQL operation and the assumption behind it. After the example, summarize the idea in one plain-language sentence before moving on.

slides.title: Diagnosis dashboard object
slides.transcript: The diagnosis dashboard is a good materialized-view example. Its grain and measures are stable. The summary may be read frequently. And leadership can tolerate a documented refresh interval. The materialized view becomes a small data product with both a schema contract and a freshness contract. Choose the smallest reusable object that matches the need. A CTE is local to one query, a view centralizes live logic, and a materialized view persists a snapshot. Promote logic into shared objects when it is stable, reused, and worth governing as part of the analytical architecture.

slides.title: Object catalog
slides.transcript: An analytics layer should be discoverable. This query lists views and materialized views in the analytics schema. Object catalogs help teams understand what reusable interfaces already exist before creating duplicates. They also support documentation and governance. Choose the smallest reusable object that matches the need. A CTE is local to one query, a view centralizes live logic, and a materialized view persists a snapshot. Promote logic into shared objects when it is stable, reused, and worth governing as part of the analytical architecture.

slides.title: Architecture review questions
slides.transcript: Before publishing a reusable object, review more than the SQL. State the grain. Review what the interface exposes. Document freshness. Inspect dependencies. And identify ownership of the business definition and operational process. These questions turn a view from an ad hoc query into a maintainable interface. A standard view stores a query definition, not a separate copy of the rows. Treat the selected columns, names, types, and grain as a contract with downstream users. Changing that contract can break dashboards or applications even if the underlying query still runs.

slides.title: Recognition checkpoint
slides.transcript: Use this checkpoint to connect requirements with objects. Temporary stages suggest a CTE. Shared live relational logic suggests a standard view. An expensive summary with acceptable refresh delay suggests a materialized view. A controlled filtered one-table interface may use an updatable view and check option. slides.title: Freshness checkpoint
slides.transcript: Freshness is one of the clearest differences among these objects. A later CTE statement uses current source data. A standard view reads through to the current underlying data. A materialized view stays at its last snapshot until refreshed. Consumers should never have to guess which freshness model they are using. slides.title: Module 12 takeaways
slides.transcript: These are the key habits from Module 12. Treat important views as contracts. Separate stable reusable meaning from report-specific logic. Understand whether a view is writable. slides.title: Object decision guide
slides.transcript: Use this decision guide when designing modular SQL. Choose a CTE for statement-local stages. Choose a standard view for stable shared live logic. Use a simple updatable view only when write behavior is intentional. Use views with proper privileges for controlled interfaces. Choose a materialized view when storing a reusable result is worth the freshness tradeoff. Keep highly changeable report thresholds outside stable shared objects. Choose the smallest reusable object that matches the need. A CTE is local to one query, a view centralizes live logic, and a materialized view persists a snapshot. Promote logic into shared objects when it is stable, reused, and worth governing as part of the analytical architecture.
